titulo.texto: Recreation of the Santa Isabel Iztapan II Mammoth

frase_gancho.texto: A giant trapped in the mud, surrounded by hunters.

puente_narrativo.texto: From giants we move on to artists. The next display case holds a piece that is tiny compared to the mammoth, but far older in meaning: a bone carved with the face of an animal.

guion_corto.texto: This scene recreates one of the great discoveries of Mexican archaeology: the mammoth of Santa Isabel Iztapan, on the shores of the ancient Lake Texcoco. An imperial mammoth, more than three meters tall, became trapped in the mud about eleven thousand years ago, and a group of hunters killed it and butchered it right there. We know this because among its bones appeared the stone points used to attack it and the knives used to cut the meat. It was decisive proof: in Mexico, people and mammoths had coexisted. For those bands, an animal like this meant meat for many weeks, hides for warmth, and bones for tools.

guion_largo.texto:
It all began with a ditch. In 1952, some workers were digging for a drainage channel in the town of Santa Isabel Iztapan, near Texcoco, and stumbled upon enormous bones. INAH specialists were called in, among them the archaeologist Luis Aveleyra and the paleontologist Manuel Maldonado-Koerdell, and they confirmed that the bones belonged to a mammoth. Among the bones of the first specimen, something unexpected also appeared: stone tools. Two years later, about three hundred and fifty meters away, a second mammoth came to light, the one we now know as Mammoth 2, and with it came the missing proof: projectile points between the ribs, of the Lerma and Angostura types, and a knife. It was textbook evidence: the hunters had killed and butchered the animal, and had left their weapons there.

To understand the value of that discovery, we need to recall the debate of the time. In the United States, the finds at Folsom and Clovis, in the 1920s and 1930s, had already shown that human beings were hunting extinct animals. In Mexico, the proof was missing. Iztapan gave it to the country: here too, more than ten thousand years ago, there were people in the valley.

Try to imagine that landscape. The Valley of Mexico was a series of shallow lakes, surrounded by cold grasslands and pine forests. There were horses, bison, camelids, giant sloths, and mammoths. The hunters, in small bands, took advantage of the muddy shores: an animal weighing several tons sank into the mud and became vulnerable. Even so, killing one was extremely dangerous and required absolute cooperation. And watch out for the picture we have in our heads: these bands did not live on mammoth all year round. They gathered plants, hunted rabbits and deer, and a mammoth was a kind of jackpot, the kind people talk about for generations.

Every part of the animal had a use. The meat was eaten fresh or dried. The hide served for warmth and for covering tents. The tendons were cord, and the bones, tools and support. The tusks, made of ivory, could be carved. Even today, when paleontologists clean a skeleton like this, they find cut marks on the bones that tell, almost like a document, how the butchering was done.

There is a thread that connects this mammoth with the courtyard where you began. That pond in the museum recalls Lake Texcoco, and this animal died on its shore, thousands of years before Tenochtitlan existed. The same lake saw the mammoth, the hunters, the villages of Tlatilco, and the Mexica capital. When you return to the light of the courtyard, look at the water with that memory.

Finally, an uncomfortable question: why did mammoths disappear? It is still debated. The climate warmed at the end of the last ice age, the grasslands changed, and the hunters may have accelerated a decline that was already underway. What is certain is that, after their disappearance, the life of the bands had to change. And that change, made of seeds, polished stone, and patience, is the thread this hall follows all the way to agriculture.

texto.Culture: Hunter-gatherers of the Lithic Stage; species Mammuthus imperator Leidy
texto.Material: Dismembered fossil mammoth skeleton, associated with Lerma and Angostura stone points, set into a diorama
texto.Origin: Santa Isabel Iztapan, Texcoco, State of Mexico

texto.pregunta: Myth: The mammoth fell into a pit trap built by the Aztecs.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It died about eleven thousand years ago on the shore of a lake, at the hands of Pleistocene hunters, thousands of years before the Aztecs existed.
